title: Old Czech through a rotating column of whole word cards
method:
The plaintext is the start of Jan Hus's Old Czech Postilla, completed in 1413, from the pinned C-059 Erben edition. Normalize to NFC lowercase and keep only letters. In the disjoint second half, rank the adjacent two-letter sequences by frequency and alphabetic ties. The 128 leading pairs receive table entries, as do all 41 single letters. At each location use the pair if it has an entry, or consume one letter. Rank the entries by their frequencies after this split in the calibration half.

Eight table columns each have four homophones per entry, with draw weights 4, 2, 1, 1. From the certain training portion of the public ZL practice split take the 5,408 most frequent eligible types (two to eleven EVA-basic glyphs, ties by spelling). Sort cards by initial glyph, final glyph, glyph count and spelling. Assign consecutive blocks of cards to successive columns. Within each column rank by training frequency and spelling, and assign successive sets of four homophones to the entries in descending plaintext calibration frequency. These rules apply to all symbols without a named exception. Choose line lengths from the corresponding public training line kind. Retain one column through a line, advance cyclically at each line break, and continue the normalized Czech stream without resetting words at the break. The book layout supplies only the line slots and their kinds. The four-word copy guard excludes forbidden homophones using the full public ZL transliteration. The guard excluded zero candidate choices in the submitted specimen.

The locally chosen primary seed 408 was fixed before the practice test. It yields 5,225 lines, 38,767 tokens and exact recovery of all 60,905 input letters from the included table with globally distinct aliases. The recovered material is the normalized letter stream. The paired controls randomize the same column schedule over token slots, randomize the card banks, or shuffle ciphertext order inside each original line. The first two encipher the identical normalized letters and each control preserves the same line lengths.

Historical components include digrams and homophones in the 1429 Alfonso V cipher, discussed by Marco Vito, pp. 259–260, https://archiviodistatomantova.cultura.gov.it/fileadmin/risorse/Pubblicazioni/Opuscoli/NAM_N._21._7._VITO_La_crittografia_diplomatica_e_militare_nell_Italia_del_Quattrocento.pdf . The whole-word cards have an analogue in Trithemius's Polygraphia III, printed in 1518, as described by Jürgen Hermes, section 2, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper7.pdf . The eight-bank, line-wise combination is an experimental construction.

Practice outcome for seed 408 was 4/28, F-009, F-017, F-024 and F-031. Raw cross-word edge MI was 0.108252 bits, versus 0.229923 for the public manuscript and 0.048092, 0.046091, and 0.096455 for randomized schedule, randomized bank, and within-line order controls respectively. F-002 still failed its 0.12-bit and within-line permutation criteria (p=0.065). The line-break drop was -0.023175 versus +0.173092 in the real text. Long-word page reuse was 0.061415 versus 0.310573 for the real text. F-009's randomized-page comparison passed at p=0.005, although its absolute reuse share was much smaller. The sensitivity seed kept the weak edge result at 0.103104 and the drop reversed at -0.063649. The three paired controls retained the same output line layout. Seed 409 samples fresh line lengths.
